questions.question: What does one coordinate in a bag-of-words vector represent?
options: One position in the document at which some term happens to occur
One vocabulary term, holding that term's own weight for the document
One document in the collection, holding its total length in tokens
One relevance judgment recorded for the document by an assessor

questions.question: Why are document vectors normally stored sparsely?
options: Each document uses only a tiny fraction of a vocabulary of millions of terms
Every term in the vocabulary carries an identical weight in each document
A sparse layout is what allows word order to survive into the index
Dense arrays cannot hold the fractional values that tf-idf produces

questions.question: For vocabulary [database, index, query], what raw-count vector represents 'index database index'?
What information does a basic bag-of-words representation discard?
options: The identity of each term that the document actually contains
The number of times each retained term occurs in the document
The membership of each document term in the indexed vocabulary
The order in which the retained terms appear in the document

questions.question: A query contains only 'car' and a document contains only 'automobile'. Why is their basic lexical dot product zero?
options: No coordinate is nonzero in both vectors, so nothing is added
The two vectors have identical norms, which cancel in the sum
The document is shorter than the query, so its weights vanish
Both terms are removed as stop words before the vectors are built

questions.question: Which change most directly alters the geometry before scoring?
options: Raising the number of results shown on the first page of output
Caching the ranked list so repeated queries skip the scorer
Merging inflected forms of a word onto one axis during stemming
Reordering the postings within each list by document identifier

questions.topic: Cosine Similarity as a Ranking Function
questions.question: What does the dot product sum?
options: The lengths of every candidate document that shares a query term
The distances between the identifiers of the matched query terms
The weights of the terms present in the document but not the query
The products of the matching query and document weights, term by term

questions.topic: Cosine Similarity as a Ranking Function
questions.question: What does cosine similarity primarily compare?
options: The number of distinct terms each of the two vectors contains
The direction of the two vectors once magnitude is divided out
The difference in token length between query and document
The overlap of the two vectors before any weighting is applied

questions.topic: Cosine Similarity as a Ranking Function
questions.question: If q = [1, 0] and d = [3, 0], what is their cosine similarity?
options: One third

questions.topic: Cosine Similarity as a Ranking Function
questions.question: Why may a ranker omit the query norm when comparing documents for one query?
options: The query norm is always exactly one after the terms are weighted
The query norm is equal to the norm of every candidate document
It is one constant for every candidate, so the order is unchanged
It is recomputed per document, so it cancels inside the numerator

questions.topic: Cosine Similarity as a Ranking Function
questions.question: Two documents have equal dot products with a query. Under cosine, which one ranks higher?
options: The one whose terms appear in more of the collection's documents
The one whose postings were written most recently into the index
The one carrying the larger Euclidean norm over its weighted terms
The one carrying the smaller positive norm over its weighted terms

questions.question: What retrieval bias does document length normalization address?
options: Rare terms receive weights so large that common terms stop mattering
Long documents can win simply by repeating query terms out of verbosity
Short queries supply too few terms for a norm to be computed at all
Posting lists lose the document identifiers needed for the merge

questions.question: What does full cosine normalization divide a document's contribution by?
options: Its Euclidean norm, computed over its weighted term values
Its collection frequency, summed across the terms it holds
Its token count in the body field, taken before weighting
Its age in days since indexing, used as a freshness divisor

questions.question: In normalization by document norm raised to alpha, what does alpha equal to zero mean?
options: Full cosine normalization is applied to every candidate
Documents above the average length are dropped entirely
The document norm is squared before dividing the score
No document-norm penalty is applied to the raw score

questions.question: Why should title and body fields usually have separate length statistics?
options: A title is guaranteed to hold every term found in the body
Their typical lengths and evidence value differ widely
Body text needs no normalizing because it is already long
Both fields converge on one average length as a corpus grows

questions.question: Using denominator (1-s)+s*length/average, what is the denominator for s=0.2, length=1000, and average=500?
Why must stored norms be versioned with tokenizer and weighting changes?
options: Versioning is what forces every stored vector to become dense
A tokenizer change cannot alter the token count of a document
Old norms and new term weights combine into incoherent scores
Stored norms are what fix the spelling used in the vocabulary
